previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of ankylosing spondylitis, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, asthma, and obesity, was admitted for a 2.5-week worsening of left lower back and sacroiliac pain consistent with an inflammatory flare. He had received 60 mg of prednisone at an outside hospital with partial relief and reported associated eye irritation concerning for possible iritis. On admission, he was treated with continued OxyContin, oxycodone for breakthrough pain, lidocaine patch, and a short course of prednisone with GI protection using sucralfate and omeprazole. Ophthalmology evaluated his eye symptoms and found no evidence of iritis, attributing the discomfort to dry eyes. His pain improved during the hospitalization, and he was discharged home on a tapering dose of prednisone, sucralfate, acetaminophen, and his baseline medications, with instructions to follow up with his primary care provider and rheumatology for long-term management.

ACUTE ISSUES
============
# Lower back and flank pain 
# Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS)
# Chronic pain on narcotics
History of AS with recurrent exacerbations requiring admission 
for pain control. In discussion with his outpatient 
rheumatologist, flares are atypical for AS (it is more typically 
chronic/indolent), and it is unlikely that inflammatory flares 
or exacerbations of AS explain his pain. He presented with his 
usual symptoms of increased back pain, which he attributes to 
inflammation, given that the appearance of symptoms corresponds 
to attempting to taper prednisone < 60mg/day. Given patient 
declines treatment with biologics for AS due to prior 
complications, these flares have been treated symptomatically 
with steroids and his home opioid regimen. The risks of chronic 
prednisone therapy were expressly discussed with the patient on 
this admission.  He felt strongly that steroids were the only 
thing that helped him, and as he has not had a major infection 
while on steroids, he finds their risks acceptable.  

Obtained plain films of T and L spine which showed no 
compression fracture. Patient with normal CTU in ___

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

You were admitted to the hospital with worsening left flank pain 
after taping your steroids at home.

Unfortunately, we did not identify a clear reason why you 
continue to have these flares. We consulted the chronic pain 
service to provide recommendations: NSAIDS (like Advil) and a 
muscle relaxant (which we prescribed).

We are discharging you on a long, slow taper of prednisone. You 
will start at 60mg a day and decrease by 5mg every 3 days. 
Because of how long this course is, we are starting calcium and 
vitamin D to prevent bone damage, and the antibiotic Bactrim to 
prevent infection.

It was a privilege to care for you in the hospital, and we wish 
you all the best.

Sincerely,

Your ___ Health Team
